summary: Hebrew marks a definite noun with the prefix ha- (הַ), written onto the noun: בַּיִת “a house” → הַבַּיִת “the house”. There is no indefinite article: a bare noun is indefinite (זֶה סֵפֶר “this is a book”; זֶה הַסֵּפֶר “this is the book”). The article usually doubles the next consonant with a dagesh (הַסֵּפֶר, הַשֻּׁלְחָן, הַמְּנוֹרָה); before the gutturals, which cannot be doubled, its vowel changes: הָ before א, ע, ר (הָאָרוֹן, הָעֵט, הָאִשָּׁה), הַ with no doubling before ה and ח (הַחֶדֶר, הַחַלּוֹן), and הֶ before חָ (הֶחָבֵר). Words that agree with a definite noun after it take the article too (הַסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה; later הַסֵּפֶר הַחָדָשׁ). From lesson 7 a definite direct object is also introduced by אֶת (הוּא קוֹרֵא אֶת הַסֵּפֶר).

askYourself: Is the thing specific — already known to the listener, or the only one? → add הַ; if not, use the bare noun (there is no “a”).
What is the first letter of the noun? א / ע / ר → הָ; ה / ח → הַ without a dagesh; חָ → הֶ; any other letter → הַ + a dagesh in that letter.
Is there a demonstrative (or later an adjective) after the noun? It takes the article too: הַסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה.
Is it a name or a noun with a possessive suffix? → it is already definite: no הַ.
Is the definite noun the direct object of a verb (from lesson 7)? → put אֶת before it.
Is it a construct phrase (two nouns, like תַּפּוּחַ אֲדָמָה)? → the article goes on the last noun: תַּפּוּחַ הָאֲדָמָה.
steps: Choose the form of the article from the first letter.
Repeat the article on a demonstrative or adjective after the noun.
Add אֶת if it is a definite direct object.

traps: No indefinite article: “a book” is just סֵפֶר — never *אֶחָד סֵפֶר as an article.
The article changes before gutturals: הָאָרוֹן, הָעֵט, הֶחָבֵר — but הַחֶדֶר, הַחֲבֵרִים.
Article on both words: הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה, not *בַּיִת הַזֶּה or *הַבַּיִת זֶה.
זֶה הַבַּיִת (“this is the house”) and הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה (“this house”) are different: the first is a sentence.
אֶת only before a definite object (lesson 7): הוּא קוֹרֵא סֵפֶר (no אֶת), but הוּא קוֹרֵא אֶת הַסֵּפֶר.
Names and nouns with a possessive suffix are already definite and take no הַ.

blocks.caption: The forms of the article (the stored DEF cells of every noun).

items.title: Indefinite — no article
points: זֶה בַּיִת — this is a house
זֹאת דִּירָה — this is a flat

items.title: Definite — הַ
points: זֶה הַבַּיִת — this is the house
הַדִּירָה פֹּה — the flat is here

blocks.title: No word for “a”
blocks.text: Do not translate “a” with אֶחָד / אַחַת (“one”) — that means “one”. “A key” is simply מַפְתֵּחַ.

blocks.title: The article repeats
blocks.text: A demonstrative after a definite noun takes the article too: הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה, הָאִשָּׁה הַהִיא. Adjectives will do the same (lesson 16).

blocks.title: Already definite
blocks.text: Names (דָּוִד, שָׂרָה) and nouns with a possessive suffix (שְׁמִי “my name”) are definite without הַ.

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Is the thing specific — known to the listener, or the only one?
What is the first letter of the noun?
Is there a demonstrative after it?

seeAlso.note: Arabic الـ is the same idea, a prefix; both languages double the next consonant — Arabic for the “sun letters” (الشَّمْس aš-šams), Hebrew for almost every letter (הַשֻּׁלְחָן). Arabic marks the indefinite with -un (tanwīn); Hebrew leaves it bare.
German has both articles, der / die / das and ein / eine, and they show gender and case; Hebrew הַ shows neither.
Chinese has no articles: definiteness comes from context, word order or 这 / 那.
